1.2 — The Unity Editor Tour

Before you write a line of code you need to read the tool that runs everything. Unity is five windows, one Inspector, and a trap called play mode. Ten minutes of tour saves ten hours of confusion.

Tour ~20 min

Open the Overworld scene. Find and name all five panes:

PaneWhat it showsYour move
Hierarchy (left)Every GameObject in this scene, as a treeClick things. Some are parents with children — why?
Scene (center)The world, editable from aboveScroll to zoom, right-drag to pan, F to focus
GameWhat the camera sees when you press PlaySwitch back and forth with the tabs
Inspector (right)Everything about the selected object — as componentsSelect the Player and read the list
Project (bottom)The repo's actual files: Scenes, Scripts, Prefabs, ArtworkNavigate to Assets/Scripts and find PlayerController.cs

The one idea to remember: GameObject → Components. Select the Player in the Hierarchy and read its Inspector: a Transform (position/rotation/scale), a Rigidbody2D (physics), BoxCollider2Ds (hitboxes), a Sprite Renderer (what you see), and a Player Controller (Script). A GameObject is an empty container; components are the abilities bolted onto it. C# scripts are just one more kind of component.

Tinker: Take the player apart

In the Overworld scene, select the Player (and its child Sprite) and try each of these — run the game after every change and undo with Ctrl+Z:

  1. Select the child Sprite object under Player and uncheck its Animator. When you press Play, does the walk animation stop? What does that tell you about what is responsible for animating the character?
  2. Select the parent Player GameObject and uncheck the Player Controller component. When you press Play, what changes?
  3. Drag the player to a completely different coordinate in the Scene view while not playing. What numbers changed in the Transform component?
The Trap ~15 min
Play mode is a dream, edit mode is reality. Press Play. While the game runs, drag a Coin prefab from Assets/Prefabs into the scene. Stop the game. The coin is gone. Everything you change in play mode — positions, Inspector values, even new objects — evaporates when you press stop. Students lose whole afternoons to this every year. You will lose five minutes once, and never again.

See it happen: press Play, select the Player, and change Transform Position X to 15 in the Inspector. Your player teleports across the screen. Press stop. What position is the player at now, and where did your change go?

The safe version of that workflow: change values in play mode to experiment and test, then stop and enter the winning numbers in edit mode so they persist. Later, when we add speed knobs and detection ranges, this will be your primary live-tuning workflow.

Socratic

Why would Unity be designed so that play-mode changes vanish? (Hint: think about testing an idea fifty times a day, and what "reset to the last known good game" means.) Is this closer to a save-file system or an undo button, and why?

Ship It ~10 min

One more piece of housekeeping: scenes are files like anything else. When you move something in the Overworld, the .unity file is dirty — Ctrl+S saves the scene (look for the asterisk in the tab). Save, then commit and push: "1.2a: editor tour".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name all five panes and what each is for
  • Explain GameObject + components with the Player as the example
  • Demonstrate play-mode vanishing with your own two hands
  • Save a scene and commit + push the change
